Hypercholesterolemia

Eat fish only once a month

Counting smoking as a risk factor

Withholding a statin because of the zero

Confirmation of homozygous familial disease

The beta blocker lowers triglyceride

The rise must be familial disease

The rise means he has hypothyroidism

Evolocumab is reserved for patients refractory to drug therapy, after high-intensity statins, not as the opening regimen.
High-intensity statin

Correct. The common regimen in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia is a high-intensity statin, with ezetimibe and nicotinic acid added if needed and aggressive reduction of other vascular risk factors.
Low-intensity statin

Lipids, liver function and creatine kinase

Thyroid function and a full blood count
Thyroid function is checked before starting, to rule out hypothyroidism, but it is not the ongoing statin monitoring list.
Kidney function and potassium levels

Lifestyle remains important, but continuing the statin is reasonable in her secondary prevention.
Continuing it is reasonable

Statins are stopped at 75
Age alone does not end therapy; continuing a well-tolerated high-intensity statin after 75 is reasonable.
Switch to a fibrate instead

Gemfibrozil is a fibrate for triglyceride lowering; his remaining problem is low-density lipoprotein.
Stop the statin
The statin is working and remains the backbone; the question is what to add, not whether to stop.
Change nothing

Add ezetimibe

opts: Add ezetimibe

Add evolocumab
Evolocumab is considered only after ezetimibe has been added to the maximal statin, and it is less cost-effective.
Add niacin
Niacin raises high-density lipoprotein best, but the add-on for persistent low-density lipoprotein on a maximal statin is ezetimibe.
Stop the statin
Stopping her statin would remove the backbone of secondary prevention; the next step adds to it.

opts: Add a fibrate or niacin

Stop the statin and watch
The statin achieved the primary target and stays; the residual triglyceride is treated in addition.
Continue with no change

Begin apheresis sessions

opts: Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
Chylomicronemia raises triglyceride usually above 1000 with eruptive papules and pancreatitis, not matched elevations with palmar xanthomas.
Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The heterozygous cholesterol disorder has normal triglyceride and tendon xanthomas, not palmar ones.
Metabolic syndrome
Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed from three of five clinical criteria and has no palmar xanthomas or apolipoprotein E2 link.
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia

Correct. An apolipoprotein E mutation with apolipoprotein E2 homozygosity lets chylomicron and very-low-density remnants accumulate, raising triglyceride and total cholesterol both to 250 to 500, with distinctive palmar xanthomas.

The receptor mutation is inherited and lifelong, so risk-factor control and therapy continue indefinitely.
Stop smoking and cut saturated fat
Correct. Treatment includes aggressive reduction of associated vascular risk factors (smoking, hypertension, diabetes) and a diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol, alongside the statin.
The statin makes diet changes unneeded
Lifestyle is the foundation of risk reduction at every step; the statin does not replace the diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol.
Smoking matters only for lung disease

Statin only after a stroke

High-intensity statin

Xanthelasmas are lipid deposits that usually indicate a genetic condition, not a reaction to cosmetics.
They suggest an inherited lipid disorder

They are harmless and need no work-up

Start a statin on these values

Order a calcium score instead

High-density cholesterol only
High-density lipoprotein is one input, but on its own it misses the cholesterol carried by the atherogenic particles.
Total cholesterol only
Total cholesterol includes the protective high-density fraction, so it is not the preferred measure here.
Triglyceride alone

High-density lipoprotein and its structural apolipoprotein A-I are protective and do not produce xanthomas.
Intermediate-density lipoprotein alone
Intermediate-density lipoprotein is the remnant after triglyceride delivery, not the particle behind eruptive xanthomas.
Chylomicrons or very-low-density lipoprotein
Correct. Eruptive xanthomas are usually seen with extremely high chylomicrons or very-low-density lipoprotein, and alcohol inhibits hepatic fatty-acid oxidation, raising triglyceride.

opts: Low-intensity statin
Low intensity lowers low-density lipoprotein under 30%, which is inadequate for secondary prevention.
Moderate-intensity statin
Moderate intensity is the fallback when high intensity is not tolerated, not the first choice after a heart attack.
Risk calculation first

High-intensity statin

set1.q: A 47-year-old man with borderline-high low-density lipoprotein asks which foods can help lower his cholesterol. Which dietary advice is most appropriate?
opts: Add more saturated and trans fat
Saturated and trans fat down-regulate hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptors and raise low-density lipoprotein, the opposite of the goal.
Eat more refined carbohydrate
Excess carbohydrate increases hepatic very-low-density triglyceride secretion, worsening the lipid profile.
Cut out all vegetables
Vegetables are among the natural sources of plant stanols and sterols, which lower cholesterol.
Add soluble fiber and plant sterols

Correct. Therapeutic lifestyle changes include less saturated fat, more soluble fiber and plant stanols or sterols, cholesterol-lowering substances found in grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds.

opts: Heavy weight lifting once a week
Occasional resistance work is not the described plan; frequent aerobic exercise 5 days a week is.
Gentle stretching on weekends only
Weekend stretching falls short of frequent aerobic exercise, which is what raises high-density lipoprotein.
Complete rest until levels improve
Physical inactivity is a major coronary risk factor, and exercise, not rest, raises high-density lipoprotein.
Brisk exercise 30 minutes, 5 days a week
Correct. Frequent aerobic exercise raises high-density lipoprotein about 5%, meaning brisk exercise 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week.

Apheresis every two weeks
Apheresis is the treatment of choice in homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, a low-density lipoprotein disorder.
Very low-fat diet and a fibrate

She needs a fibrate before starting
Borderline triglyceride does not call for a fibrate; monitoring is the advised response to starting estrogen.
Her lipids should be monitored

Estrogen lowers all her lipids

set2.q: A 41-year-old man has a high-density lipoprotein of 32 mg/dL. He smokes a pack a day and is 30 pounds overweight. Which single change can raise his high-density lipoprotein by up to 10%?
opts: Moderate alcohol
Alcohol is to be limited to moderate consumption; it is not the change that raises high-density lipoprotein up to 10%.
Low-carbohydrate diet
Carbohydrate restriction lowers hepatic very-low-density triglyceride output; the rise of up to 10% in high-density lipoprotein comes from stopping smoking.
Taking a fibrate
Fibrates raise high-density lipoprotein 10% to 30% but are drugs, not a lifestyle change; stopping smoking gives up to 10%.
Smoking cessation
Correct. Smoking cessation increases high-density lipoprotein up to 10%; losing 6 pounds raises it about 1 mg/dL, and frequent aerobic exercise about 5%.

Correct. If the injectable class is considered, ezetimibe is added to the maximal statin before it; skipping that step is out of sequence and less cost-effective.
Adding ezetimibe to the statin
Adding ezetimibe is the reasonable next step when low-density lipoprotein stays 70 or more on a maximal statin.
Continuing the maximal statin
The maximal statin stays in place; nonstatin drugs are added on top of it rather than substituted for it.
Rechecking lipids after the change

set2.q: A 9-year-old boy has untreated homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, and testing shows under 2% of normal low-density lipoprotein receptor activity. His parents ask about the outlook without treatment. Which answer is accurate?
opts: Pancreatitis is the main threat
Pancreatitis is the danger of very high triglyceride; his disorder kills through accelerated atherosclerosis.
Survival past the second decade is rare
Correct. Untreated receptor-negative patients (under 2% of normal activity) rarely survive past the second decade, and accelerated atherosclerosis can cause sudden death in childhood.
Heart disease is unlikely before 60
Disease comes decades earlier: symptomatic atherosclerosis before puberty is typical of the homozygous form.
He will outgrow the disorder
The receptor defect is inherited from both parents and lifelong, so it is not outgrown with age.

Loss of vision

A premature heart attack

Diet cannot change it

Cut excess carbohydrate

Nephrotic syndrome and anorexia
Nephrotic syndrome and anorexia nervosa are rule-outs when low-density lipoprotein is elevated.
Pancreatitis and gallstones
Neither is a rule-out before a statin; pancreatitis is a complication of very high triglyceride.
Diabetes, smoking and obesity
Correct. With low high-density lipoprotein, rule out diabetes mellitus, cigarette smoking and obesity, then address them as the main levers.

opts: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises triglyceride and total cholesterol together to 250 to 500 with palmar xanthomas.
Severe hypertriglyceridemia

Mixed dyslipidemia

set2.q: A 64-year-old man has had both a heart attack and an ischemic stroke. On a maximal statin plus ezetimibe his low-density lipoprotein is 88 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Add evolocumab or alirocumab

Correct. In very high-risk disease, if low-density lipoprotein stays 70 or more on a maximally tolerated statin and ezetimibe, adding a proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor is reasonable.
Replace the statin with a fibrate
Fibrates lower triglyceride; replacing the statin would remove his most effective low-density therapy.
No change, as he is below 100
Below 100 is not the target in very high-risk disease; the threshold for adding nonstatin therapy is 70.
Add a bile acid sequestrant only
Sequestrants are adjuncts, but the next step after statin plus ezetimibe in very high-risk disease is the injectable class.

His diet alone explains the low value
Diet affects lipids, but his anabolic steroid use is a known cause of decreased high-density lipoprotein.
The steroids are lowering his good cholesterol

Low values like his carry no heart risk

Test only if xanthomas appear

At 50 mg/dL or more it is a risk-enhancing factor and calls for aggressive low-density lowering.
He needs aggressive low-density lowering

It is protective and lowers his risk

set2.q: A 48-year-old man without cardiovascular disease has hypertension and smokes. His clinician wants to estimate his 10-year risk of atherosclerotic disease to guide statin therapy. Which tool is appropriate?
opts: Pooled Cohort Equation

Correct. It estimates 10-year primary risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease in patients 40 to 79 without pre-existing disease, using variables such as age, sex, cholesterol, systolic pressure, diabetes and smoking.
Skin biopsy for receptors
Skin biopsy confirms homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and does not estimate population risk.
Fundoscopic examination
Fundoscopy finds lipemia retinalis in chylomicronemia and has no role in 10-year risk estimation.
Metabolic syndrome criteria
The syndrome's five criteria define a diagnosis; they do not give a 10-year risk percentage.

Abandoning therapy after a heart attack leaves him unprotected; the fallback is a moderate-intensity statin.
Fish oil in place of statins
Fish oil is associated with lower coronary death but does not replace statin therapy in secondary prevention.
A fibrate instead

About 60 to 80 pounds

opts: Thyroid function tests

Refer for liver transplantation
Transplantation is considered for the homozygous disorder, which lacks receptors; she is heterozygous and has not exhausted drug options.
